articleTitle: Computationally efficient model of the basilar membrane
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Techniques for Speech Processing
abstract: Describes a digital filter model of the basilar membrane (BM). The model incorporates mechanical features of the BM which govern frequency selectivity. The important feature is the inclusion of the mechanical properties of the tectorial membrane (TM) and the stereocilia of the outer hair cells (OHC). This results in an improved lower frequency selectivity as well as improvements to the phase curve.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Optimal frame rate analysis for speech recognition
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Techniques for Speech Processing
abstract: The authors examine the process of sampling the underlying time-frequency distribution and show that the degree of smoothing applied to each estimate involves a trade-off between minimising the bias and the variance. This leads naturally to the use of a time variant smoothing window and a mean square error criterion for determining the optimum window spread function. They also present some preliminary results from applying these ideas to the speech recognition problem.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Excitation analysis and modelling for high quality speech synthesis
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Techniques for Speech Processing
abstract: Describes work which is aimed at improving the naturalness of copy synthesised female speech produced using a software implementation of the JSRU parallel formant synthesiser. The motivation behind this work is drawn from a number of recent publications which show that excitation specific effects relating to the shape of the excitation spectrum contribute significantly to the naturalness of synthetic female speech. An attempt is made to model a number of known excitation effects by dynamically changing the voice mix and mark-space ratio control signals using information obtained from a laryngographic signal. To accommodate such excitation effects, modifications are made to the bandwidth and frequency values stored in the synthesisers parameter control file. Copy synthetic speech produced using a number of different parameter combinations are compared through subjective testing and results presented.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Parallel algorithms for automatic speech recognition
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Techniques for Speech Processing
abstract: In the research, neural nets, or to be more precise, multilayer perceptrons (MLP), are used for the nonlinear phonetic mapping of the acoustic features. These phonetic outputs are used, subsequently, for the final probabilistic computation of the hidden Markov models (HMM). The speech recognition system was implemented and tested on real speech, low-pass filtered with a cut-off frequency of 3.8 kHz, and sampled at 8 kHz.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Single and multiple channel approaches to speech enhancement
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Techniques for Speech Processing
abstract: A description of two recently developed techniques for enhancing speech is presented. The first is a single channel approach where an optimum filter is found given a priori knowledge of the noise and the noisy speech models. The filter computation involves the solution of a single diophantine equation. The second is a two channel approach which can be extended to multiple channels. The microphones are placed 10 cm apart and the acoustic path transfer function between the two microphones is identified during a noise only period. The resulting output is shown to be a noise reduced but slightly filtered speech signal. Results are given to compare the two approaches in terms of SNR improvements and quality of the resulting processed signal.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Speech recognition using peak frequency representations
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Techniques for Speech Processing
abstract: Signal processing for speech recognition combines two distinct elements, spectral estimation, and feature selection. The author separates the issues of estimating the spectrum from that of describing it to a speech recogniser. He focuses on providing a description in terms of the frequencies of peaks. A minimum squared error criterion is used for specifying the description, but it is entirely distinct from that underlying LPC analysis, and is optimised by a dynamic programming technique.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A comparison of distance measures for speech segmentation in variable frame rate speech vocoding
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Techniques for Speech Processing
abstract: Compares three different formulations of spectral transitivity function based on LPC derived coefficients and assesses their suitability for speech segmentation in a variable frame rate (VFR) vocoder. The first of these formulations was proposed for a variable frame rate vocoder and the other two were proposed for speech recognition and verification systems. The quality of VFR vocoded speech has been compared with that of a fixed frame rate vocoder and some suggestions are made for further improvements to the segmentation, on the basis of this comparison.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Intermediate level speech processing as an aim of low level signal analysis
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Techniques for Speech Processing
abstract: In the general area of speech recognition, two processing levels have dominated recent literature: low-level signal processing aimed at segmenting and spectrally analysing speech input; and high-level syntactic and semantic processing, part of natural language processing (NLP). Both areas cover vital aspects of speech, but they do not readily link together. Greater activity is needed to link these two into complete systems. The linkage of the two is taken to define an intermediate speech processing level. The authors examine the processes which constitute this interface (they are disambiguation processes), reporting on the phenome lattice as the end-product of the signal processing level.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A CELP codebook and search technique using a Hopfield net
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Techniques for Speech Processing
abstract: A new method of structuring a ternary excitation codebook for a CELP coder is introduced in which the main codebook is divided into several sub-codebooks. It is shown how a modified Hopfield neural net is capable of searching such a codebook and selecting a near optimum code-vector. Hence an algorithm is derived which offers considerable computational savings over previously proposed codebook search methods. Results are presented demonstrating the net's performance and its effect on the subjective quality of the coded speech.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Techniques for Speech Processing
abstract: Presents a review of the development of speech processing technology. The beginning of speech processing can conveniently be dated to the invention of the vocoder in 1939. Each of the basic application areas, coding, synthesis and recognition has grown and diverged as new applications have emerged. Two important applications are speech recognition over the telephone network and recognition of computer input.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
